title: Sorting and Data: Picture Graphs
seo_title: Foundation Data Worksheets: Sorting, Counting and Picture Graphs (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations.
meta_desc: Free Foundation (Prep, Kindergarten) maths worksheets on sorting and data, matched to the Australian Curriculum (AC9MFST01): sort and count, sorting rules, picture graphs, most and fewest, and asking questions. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Collect, sort, then count to answer a question.
key_sub: In a picture graph each picture is one thing. The longest row has the most.
body_html:
Sort, then count

To answer a question, collect the data (ask, look or count), sort it into groups, then count each group.

Picture graphs

A picture graph shows each answer as one picture. The longest row has the most. The shortest row has the fewest.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Counting everything instead of one kindSort first, then count one group
Reading the longest row as the fewestLongest row means the most
Giving one of the counts for 'how many more'Find the difference between the rows

faq.q: What data do Foundation students learn about?
faq.a: They collect, sort and compare data shown with objects and pictures to answer simple questions about familiar things, like the class's favourite fruit (AC9MFST01).
A graph where each picture stands for one thing or one person. Rows of pictures make it easy to see which group has the most.
A question you can answer by collecting data, such as: What is our class's favourite colour? or How do we get to school?

faq.q: How can I practise data at home?
faq.a: Sort the washing by colour, count the cars that go past by colour, or vote on dinner with family members and line up the votes.

items.q: The class wants to find out which fruit is the class favourite. Which is the best question to ask everyone?
c: Which fruit do you like best?
items.e: A good question asks everyone the same thing about fruit, and each answer can be counted. Which fruit do you like best?.

items.q: The class wants to know how children get to school. What should they do?
c: Count the cars in the car park
Ask every child how they get to school and count the answers
items.e: Ask everyone the same question, then sort and count the answers. Ask every child how they get to school and count the answers.

items.q: Ruby asks the class: Do you have a pet? 12 say yes and 8 say no. Did more children say yes or no?
items.e: 12 is more than 8, so more children said yes. Yes.

items.q: Mia asks: Do you have a pet? 12 say yes and 8 say no. How many children were asked?
items.e: 12 and 8 make 20 children. 20.

items.q: The class votes for a class pet name: Spot gets 9 votes and Max gets 6. Which name wins?
items.e: 9 is more than 6, so Spot wins. Spot.

items.q: Spot gets 9 votes and Max gets 6. How many more votes does Spot get?
items.e: 9 take away 6 is 3: Spot gets 3 more votes. 3.

items.q: Which question could you answer by asking your classmates?
c: How many fish are in the sea?
What will the weather be next year?
How far away is the Moon?
items.e: You can ask your classmates about their favourite colour and count the answers. What colour is your favourite?.

items.q: Mei wants to know the class's favourite sport. 5 chose footy, 7 chose swimming and 3 chose cricket. Which sport is the favourite?
items.e: 7 is the biggest number, so swimming is the favourite. Swimming.

items.q: 5 chose footy, 7 chose swimming and 3 chose cricket. Which sport did the fewest choose?
items.e: 3 is the smallest number, so the fewest chose cricket. Cricket.

items.q: The class sorts their lunches into sandwiches and wraps. There are 11 sandwiches and 7 wraps. How many lunches altogether?
items.e: 11 and 7 make 18 lunches. 18.

items.q: Why do we sort and count data?
c: To answer a question and compare groups
Because counting is only for numbers
items.e: Sorting and counting helps us answer a question and compare groups. To answer a question and compare groups.

items.q: Jack counts the colours of the cars in the car park: 4 white, 6 red and 2 blue. Which colour is most common?
items.e: 6 is the biggest number, so red is the most common. Red.

items.q: 4 white, 6 red and 2 blue cars. How many fewer blue cars than red cars?
items.e: Red has 6 and blue has 2. 6 take away 2 is 4. 4.

items.q: Matilda asks: Do you like rain? 10 say yes and 10 say no. What can she say?
c: The same number said yes and no
items.e: 10 and 10 are the same, so the same number said yes and no. The same number said yes and no.

items.q: The class wants to know which day of the week is the favourite. What should each child do?
c: Choose one day and vote once
items.e: Each child votes once, so every vote can be counted fairly. Choose one day and vote once.

items.q: 16 children voted for their favourite colour. Blue got 9 votes and the rest chose green. How many chose green?
items.e: 16 take away 9 leaves 7 who chose green. 7.

items.q: The class sorts the toys box into balls and blocks. How should they show how many of each?
c: Put each group in a line and count
items.e: Lining up each group makes them easy to count and compare. Put each group in a line and count.

items.q: Lachlan asks 8 friends: Do you walk to school? 3 say yes. How many say no?
items.e: 8 friends, 3 say yes, so 8 take away 3 is 5 say no. 5.

items.q: Which data could you collect in your classroom?

items.e: You can look at your classmates and count, so this data can be collected in the classroom. How many children have brown hair.

items.q: The class votes for a book to read. Possum Magic gets 8 votes and the other book gets 8 votes. What can they say?
items.e: 8 and 8 are the same number of votes, so it is a tie. It is a tie.
